### Questions

What makes a chiropractor-coach different from a regular pickleball coach?

Most coaches only see your technique. I look at the whole chain that produces the shot, your legs, hips, core, and arm, and how well they're working together. Most breakdowns come from that chain firing out of order. A physical limitation shows up sometimes too, and I'll catch that along the way. Either way you get the real cause instead of a guess.

How does virtual pickleball coaching work?

Through Crestline, you send me footage of your games or drills: 2 video reviews a month on Pro, 4 on Premium. I review it and send back voice-and-video feedback with live commentary (the free trial is a written diagnosis), plus a custom drill plan built around exactly what I see. No travel, no scheduling around a court.

Do I need to live near Florida to work with you?

No. My in-person lessons and mobile chiropractic care are limited to Volusia County, FL, but virtual coaching through Crestline works with players anywhere in the world. All I need is footage of your games or drills. The coaching works the same no matter where you play.

What's included in a Crestline coaching program?

Crestline starts with a free gameplay diagnosis. Monthly plans are $99 for 2 video reviews or $199 for 4, both with voice-and-video feedback and a custom drill plan; the $199 plan adds strength, rehab, and nutrition support.

What level of player do you work with?

Mostly serious recreational players in the 3.0 to 4.0 range who are ready to break through a plateau, plus higher-level players wanting a second set of eyes on their game. Put simply: 3.5 is the intermediate rating and 4.0+ is advanced, and I coach the intermediate player who wants to get there. Not sure where you fall or if it's a fit? Just reach out and ask.

How much do lessons cost?

Team lessons for league teams and regular groups of 4 to 8 players are $70 per player: an hour on court with your games filmed and coached, then a video breakdown of each pair's film afterward, shared with your notes in a private YouTube playlist and a Google Doc you keep. Private lessons ($90 an hour) and small-group lessons ($60 per person, 2 to 3 players) are also available. Virtual coaching through Crestline starts with a free gameplay diagnosis, with monthly plans after that.

What's your cancellation policy?

For in-person lessons, I ask for at least 12 hours' notice to cancel or reschedule. Last-minute no-shows affect other players' time too. Crestline virtual coaching is a monthly subscription you can pause or cancel anytime before your next billing date.

# Why You're Stuck at 3.5: The Five Leaks (article)

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/why-youre-stuck-at-3-5/

Dr. Lane Odom · The Pickleball Chiro

## Why You’re Stuck at 3.5: The Five Leaks

You have the shots. You’re losing the same point over and over. Here’s where, and here’s the fix for each.

4.7 DUPR Doctor of Chiropractic PCI Certified Coach

By Dr. Lane Odom, DC · PCI Certified Coach · Published September 13, 2026 · Updated October 12, 2026 · 10 min read

A 3.5 player isn’t missing a shot. A 3.5 player has a leak: one shot or movement pattern that loses the same point several times a game. Most 3.0–4.0 players have exactly one, it’s almost always in the first four shots or the transition zone, and it’s why drilling harder hasn’t moved your rating.

I coach players between 3.0 and 4.0 in person across Volusia County, Florida, and virtually anywhere through game film. I’m also a Doctor of Chiropractic, so I watch the body as closely as the paddle. After a few hundred hours of lessons and film reviews, the same five leaks keep showing up. Every player I’ve seen stuck at 3.5 has at least one of them. Most have exactly one.

This article walks through all five: how each one shows up in a rec game, why it happens, and what actually fixes it. Read the whole thing, then use the self-checks to find yours. If you want it scored for you, the free 17-question diagnosis does exactly that.

### Leak 1: Your Game Is Capped Before the Rally Even Starts

The first four shots (serve, return, third shot, fourth shot) decide who gets to the kitchen line first. At 3.5, most points are effectively over before anyone dinks. If your serve is short, your return floats, or your third shot pops up, you lose the line, and the rally after that is just cleanup.

#### How it shows up

You lose a lot of points in the first three hits and can’t say why. Your third shot either sails long because you drove it from a bad position, or sits up in the kitchen because you tried to drop it without your feet set. On the return, you hit it and stand there, and now the serving team is at the line before you are.

#### Why it happens

Players learn the serve and return first, so they stop thinking about them. But at 3.5 the serve is usually short and safe, the return is hit from a flat-footed stance and not followed to the line, and the third shot is a coin flip between a drive and a drop with no rule for which one. None of those are hard shots. They’re decisions nobody made.

#### The fix

- Serve deep with margin. Aim for the back third of the box, three feet over the net. A deep serve keeps the returner back and gives you a better third ball. Stop aiming for lines.

- Return deep, then move. The return is not a shot, it’s a shot plus a sprint. Hit it deep down the middle and be at the kitchen line before their third shot bounces. If you only fix one thing in this whole article, fix this.

- Give the third shot a checklist. Drive or drop is not a feel decision, it’s three variables you read before the ball gets there: depth of the ball, height of the ball, and whether your opponents are on the line or off it. Deep, high, and opponents off the line leans drive. Short, low, and opponents already at the line leans drop. Two out of three usually decides it. The point isn’t which shot you like. It’s that you ran the checklist. (Full breakdown, with examples and a drill: Third Shot Drive or Drop? The Three-Read Checklist.)

- Drill (10 minutes): partner at the kitchen line feeds returns. You hit third-shot drops from the baseline, then follow each one in. Target: over the net by two feet, landing in the kitchen. Count how many out of ten let you get to the line.

Self-check: in your next rec game, count how many points end within the first four shots. If it’s more than half, this is your leak.

The first four shots start before anyone hits: a minute from a women’s 3.5 game I broke down, on where to stand while your partner serves.

### Leak 2: You’re Guessing Instead of Deciding

Every ball in pickleball is one decision: attack or reset. A 3.5 player doesn’t have a rule for that call, so they make it in real time under pressure, and guessing under pressure goes wrong. This isn’t athleticism or hand speed. It’s a missing framework.

#### How it shows up

You attack a ball below your waist and put it in the net. You dink a ball that was sitting up at shoulder height. Your partner says “why did you hit that?” and you don’t know. You’ll also feel it as “I didn’t mean to hit it that hard,” which is your hands making a decision your brain didn’t.

#### Why it happens

Rec play rewards hitting hard, so players build a habit of attacking anything they can reach. Nobody ever gave them the one rule that governs the whole game: where is the ball relative to the net at contact? Above the net, you can attack. Below the net, you have to lift it, and anything you lift hard becomes an easy put-away for the other side.

#### The fix

- The one rule: contact above the net tape = attack is on the table. Contact below the net tape = reset or dink, no exceptions. Say it out loud on the court for a week. It feels remedial. It works.

- Add the second filter: even on a high ball, is the opponent’s paddle up and ready? If yes, a speed-up gets countered. Attack the player whose paddle is low or who is still moving.

- Drill (10 minutes): partner feeds mixed balls, some high, some low. Before contact, you call “up” or “down” out loud, then hit the matching shot. Miss the call and the point is theirs. This moves the decision from your hands to your eyes.

Self-check: film ten of your unforced errors. If more than four were attacks on a ball below the net, this is your leak.

### Leak 3: You’re Living in No-Man’s-Land

The transition zone is the space between the baseline and the kitchen line, roughly 7 to 15 feet from the net. More points are lost there than anywhere else on the court. If you feel rushed, caught in between, or a step behind, this is almost certainly your leak, and it’s one of the fastest to fix.

#### How it shows up

You hit a third shot and then either stand still at the baseline or sprint straight to the line regardless of what you hit. The ball comes at your feet while you’re moving forward and you either pop it up or hit it out. You get “stuck” at midcourt for a whole rally, taking balls at your shoelaces.

#### Why it happens

Two missing habits: no split step, and no connection between the quality of your shot and how far you move. If your drop was good, you should be moving in. If it was high, you should be stopping and getting low, because a hard ball is coming. Most 3.5 players do the same thing either way, and the same thing is usually wrong.

#### The fix

- Split step every time the opponent hits. A small hop that lands as their paddle contacts the ball. It puts you on the balls of your feet and buys you the half second you’re currently missing.

- Move on your shot, not on a schedule. Good drop: move in behind it. Bad drop: stop, get low, paddle out front, and reset the next ball. You earn your way to the line one good shot at a time.

- Read their body, not just the ball. Your opponents at the line tell you what’s coming before they hit it. Paddles up, standing tall, leaning in: they’re about to attack, so get low and stay put and expect a hard ball at your feet. Head dropping, paddle dropping, weight going backward, looking defensive: that’s your green light to keep moving in and take the line. Most 3.5 players stare at the ball and miss all of this.

- Reset off the bounce, not out of the air. Let the low ball bounce when you can. Knees bent, paddle in front of your body, soft grip, and lift it into the kitchen. You’re not trying to win the point from midcourt. You’re trying to survive it.

- Drill (10 minutes): start at the baseline. Partner at the line hits at your feet. You must hit three resets into the kitchen before you’re allowed to move in. Any pop-up, start over. This builds the patience the zone requires.

Self-check: watch a rally where you lost. Freeze it when the point ended. If you were between 7 and 15 feet from the net, this is your leak.

### Leak 4: You’re Losing at the Line, or Never Getting There

At 4.0, points are won at the kitchen line. A 3.5 player either loses the point before reaching the line, or reaches it with no plan: aimless dinks, panicky speed-ups, hands that lose the exchange. The team that controls the line controls the game, and the soft game responds to targeted drilling faster than almost anything else.

#### How it shows up

In a dink rally, you’re just getting the ball back until someone makes a mistake, and it’s usually you. You speed up out of boredom, not opportunity. When a speed-up comes at you, your paddle is at your waist and the ball is past you. You win the line and then give it back with one impatient shot.

#### Why it happens

The dink gets taught as a defensive shot, so players dink to not lose. At 4.0 the dink is an offensive shot: it moves the opponent, pulls them off balance, and creates the high ball you’re allowed to attack. Without intent, the rally is a coin flip, and without a ready position, the speed-up is a loss before it’s hit.

#### The fix

- Dink with a target. Cross-court to the opponent’s backhand foot is your default. Every dink should make them move or reach. If they’re hitting comfortably from a balanced stance, you’re feeding them.

- Speed up only on the rule from Leak 2. Ball above the net, opponent’s paddle low or body moving. Otherwise, keep dinking. Boredom is not a green light.

- Ready position at the line: paddle up at chest height, out in front, elbows away from your body, knees bent. If your paddle is below your waist, you’ve already lost the hands battle.

- Drill (15 minutes): 20 cross-court dinks in a row with a partner, backhand to backhand, no misses or the count restarts. Then play “speed-up only on a high ball” to 11: any speed-up on a low ball is an automatic point for the other side.

Self-check: in a typical rec game, how often do you actually get to the line before the point is decided? If it’s less than half the time, or you get there and lose the dink rallies, this is your leak.

### Leak 5: Your Technique Works in Warmup. It’s Not Surviving the Match.

If your game falls apart by game three, that’s not mental toughness. The chain of legs, hips, and core that powers every shot is running out before your technique does. Pickleball’s movements (the low dig, the lateral recovery step, the controlled reset) have a physical floor most players never build off the court.

#### How it shows up

Game one you look like a 4.0. Game three your contact point drifts late, your ready position sinks to your waist, your resets start popping up, and you’re reaching for balls you were stepping to an hour ago. You’ll also feel it as the “that’s just how my body feels now” spots: a knee, a low back, a hip that doesn’t open the way it used to.

#### Why it happens

This is the leak I see most as a chiropractor, and the one players least want to hear about. Every low ball is a squat. Every lateral move is a lunge. If your hips and ankles don’t have the range, or your glutes don’t have the endurance, your body finds a cheaper way to get there: knees cave, back rounds, arm swings instead of the trunk rotating. The cheaper way is less accurate and it hurts, and fatigue makes you pick it earlier every game. The research backs the hip side of this up: a 2015 systematic review found that adding hip and glute strengthening to knee rehab reduced front-of-knee pain and improved function better than knee work alone,1 and injury data on players over 60 shows strains and sprains, most of them from slips, trips, and falls, are the leading reason pickleball players end up in an emergency department.2 The floor isn’t optional.

#### The fix

- Build the floor off the court (10 minutes, three times a week): hip hinges, lateral lunges, split-squat holds, and ankle mobility work. Not a gym program. A floor.

- Warm up before game one, not during it. Five minutes of leg swings, lateral shuffles, and a few low dinks before you play. Cold hips are the reason game one looks worse than game two.

- Stop playing through the spot that hurts. A nagging knee or a tight hip changes your footwork whether you notice or not, and it’s usually fixable. Get it looked at by someone who understands the sport.

- Drill (on court): play a game to 11 where every reset must be hit with your knees bent below your paddle. Stand up straight, lose the point. You’ll feel exactly where the floor is.

Self-check: compare your first game and your third game of the same session. If the third one has more pop-ups and late contacts, this is your leak. It can also be stacked on top of another one.

Knee pain specifically is common enough that I wrote a full breakdown of it: Pickleball Knee Pain: The 3-Stage Fix. If you're in Volusia County and want hands-on care alongside the physical work, mobile chiropractic care comes to you.

The physical section is educational, not medical advice. If something hurts, see a licensed provider. Full disclaimer in our Terms.

### How to Find Which Leak Is Yours

Two ways. The fast one: take the free 17-question diagnosis, which scores you across all five areas and tells you the lowest one. The honest one: film one rec game from behind your own baseline, watch where each lost point ended, and count. Your leak shows up inside the first ten points.

One warning. Players almost always guess wrong about their own leak. The player who thinks it’s their dinks usually has a transition-zone problem. The player who thinks they need a better drive usually needs a return they follow to the line. That’s the whole reason I coach from film: what you feel and what the camera shows are different things.

If you’ve got more than one, that’s common and it’s not a coincidence. They feed each other. A physical leak makes the transition zone worse. A shot-selection leak makes the kitchen game worse. Fix one and the next one usually gets easier.

### How the Five Leaks Map to USA Pickleball’s 4.0 Definition

USA Pickleball publishes an official skill-level definition for every rating, and the difference between its 3.5 and 4.0 descriptions is the same five leaks in different words. A 3.5 is “selectively mixing up soft shots with power shots... with inconsistent results” on the third shot; a 4.0 “consistently executes effective 3rd shot strategies.” A 3.5 is “starting to understand the block/re-set volley”; a 4.0 is “able to block hard volleys... and can consistently drop them into the NVZ.” A 3.5 makes “moderate unforced errors”; a 4.0 makes “limited unforced errors” with “strong footwork” and “excellent court position.”3

Read those side by side and the mapping is direct:

- Leak 1 (first four shots) is the 3.5 serve/return line, “places a high majority of serves/returns with varying depth,” becoming the 4.0 line, “serves with power, accuracy, and depth.” Depth is the whole difference.

- Leak 2 (shot selection) is the third-shot line: “selectively mixing... inconsistent results” versus “consistently executes effective 3rd shot strategies.” Same shots, a rule for choosing them.

- Leak 3 (transition zone) is the volley line: “starting to understand the block/re-set” versus “can consistently drop them into the NVZ.” That is the reset, on the way in.

- Leak 4 (kitchen game) is the dink line: “beginning to understand which balls are attackable” versus “playing both consistently and with offensive intent.” Patience first, then the attack.

- Leak 5 (physical) is the strategy line nobody reads as physical: “moderate unforced errors” becoming “limited unforced errors” with “strong footwork.” Errors in the fourth game are a legs problem before they are a hands problem.

So when a coach, a rating system, or a self-assessment says “you are a 3.5,” it is not a verdict on your talent. It is a list of five specific gaps, and you almost certainly only have one or two of them.

### What to Do Next

Pick your leak. Run its 10-minute drill twice a week for a month instead of playing one more rec game. That alone moves most 3.5s.

If you want my read on your specific game, that happens on Crestline: you send footage (drills are fine: serves, returns, resets, volleys, dinks), I break down exactly which leak it is and what to do about it, and you get a drill plan built around it. It works from anywhere and starts free. If you’re in Volusia County, Florida, in-person lessons are the other route.

Get My Read on Your Game → Take the Free Diagnosis →

### Questions

What does “stuck at 3.5” mean in pickleball?

A 3.5 player has the strokes (serve, return, dink, volley) but loses points in the same way over and over, so their rating stops moving even though they keep playing. The gap to 4.0 is rarely a missing shot. It is usually one pattern, a “leak,” that costs them the same point several times a game. In rating terms, 3.5 is intermediate and 4.0+ is advanced; this article is for the intermediate player trying to make that jump.

What is a “leak” in pickleball?

A leak is the one shot or movement pattern that loses you the most points. Most 3.0–4.0 players have one, and it is usually in the first four shots or the transition zone. Fixing the leak moves a rating faster than adding a new shot does.

What are the five areas where 3.5 players lose points?

The first four shots (serve, return, third, fourth), shot selection (attack vs reset), the transition zone (baseline to kitchen), the kitchen or soft game (dinks, resets, speed-ups), and the physical side (whether the body can hold technique for a full session).

How do I find out which leak is mine?

Take the free 17-question quiz at pickleballchiro.co/quiz, which scores you across all five areas, or film one rec game from behind the baseline and count where your points end. Most players’ leak shows up within the first ten points.

How long does it take to go from 3.5 to 4.0 in pickleball?

It depends on which leak you have and how much you play. Transition-zone and shot-selection leaks usually respond to targeted drilling within weeks. Physical leaks take longer because the body has to adapt. Drilling a shot that is not your leak can take months and move nothing.

# Third Shot Drive or Drop? The Three-Read Checklist (article)

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/third-shot-drive-or-drop/

Dr. Lane Odom · The Pickleball Chiro

## Third Shot Drive or Drop? The Three-Read Checklist

Stop coin-flipping your third shot. Three things to read before the ball gets to you, and a rule for what to do when they disagree.

4.7 DUPR Doctor of Chiropractic PCI Certified Coach

By Dr. Lane Odom, DC · PCI Certified Coach · Published September 14, 2026 · 8 min read

The third shot in pickleball should be a drive or a drop based on three reads: how deep the return is, how high it bounces, and whether your opponents are on the kitchen line or off it. Deep, high, and opponents off the line leans drive. Short, low, and opponents already at the line leans drop. When the reads disagree, two out of three decides.

This is the second article in the Why You’re Stuck at 3.5 series. That one covered the five leaks. This one goes deep on the first decision inside Leak 1, because in the game film I review, the third shot is the first thing I check, and it’s the decision intermediate players most often make with no rule at all.

If you’re a 3.5 trying to get to 4.0, you don’t need a better drive or a better drop. You need to stop guessing which one to hit. That’s what this checklist is for.

### Why 3.5 Players Coin-Flip the Third Shot

Most intermediate players hit the third shot they like, not the one the ball asked for. Drivers drive everything and drop when they’re scared. Droppers drop everything and drive when they’re frustrated. Neither one is reading the ball, so neither one gets better at the decision, no matter how many they hit.

#### How it shows up

Your drive sails long or gets volleyed back at your feet because you hit it off a low ball with two people already at the line. Or your drop sits up in the kitchen because you tried to feather a deep, shoulder-high return with your feet still moving. Same player, both errors, same game. The shot wasn’t the problem. The choice was.

#### Why it happens

Nobody gave you a rule. Coaches say “drop when they’re at the line, drive when they’re not,” which is one read out of three, and it’s the read you have the least time to make. So you fall back on preference. The fix is not a new shot. It’s three questions you answer in the half second before contact, every single time, until you don’t have to think about them.

### Read 1: How Deep Is the Ball?

Depth is where the return lands relative to your baseline. A deep return that pushes you back behind the line leans drive. A short return that lets you step in and take the ball inside the baseline leans drop, because you’re closer to the kitchen and the drop is a shorter, easier shot.

#### What to look for

Watch the return come off their paddle and ask one thing: am I moving backward or forward to get to it? Backward means deep. Forward means short. That’s the whole read. You don’t need to judge feet and inches.

#### Why it matters

This is the read most players get backwards. They think a short ball is a gift to drive. But a short ball puts you closer to the net, and closer to the net is exactly where a drop becomes easy and a drive becomes a pop-up waiting to happen. A deep ball is the opposite: you’re far from the kitchen, a drop has to travel a long way and stay low the whole trip, and a drive off a deep ball can be hit with margin and still be hard to handle.

### Read 2: How High Is the Ball?

Height is where the ball is when you make contact, relative to the net. A ball you contact above net height leans drive, because you can hit down or flat on it. A ball you contact below net height leans drop, because driving it means lifting it, and a lifted drive is the easiest ball in pickleball to counter.

#### What to look for

Where is your paddle at contact: above your waist or below your knee? Waist and up is a high ball. Knee and down is a low ball. Between is a judgment call, which is why you need the other two reads.

#### Why it matters

The net is 34 inches in the middle. If you contact the ball below that, a drive has to go up before it goes down, and a player at the line will block it back at your feet. Intermediate players drive low balls constantly because the ball “felt” hittable. It was hittable. It just wasn’t driveable. Below the net tape, the drop is almost always the higher-percentage shot.

### Read 3: Are They on the Line or Off It?

The third read is your opponents’ position. If both of them are already at the kitchen line, a drive has to beat two blockers with almost no time to react, so the read leans drop. If either one is still off the line, in the transition zone or hanging back, a drive at that player’s feet leans drive.

#### What to look for

Look up before you hit, not after. Specifically look at the returner, because that’s the player who has to cover the most ground. Are they still moving forward? Did they stop at midcourt? A returner who hit and stood there is the best drive target in the game.

#### Why it matters

This is the read everyone teaches, and it’s the right one, but on its own it’s incomplete. Two players at the line with a deep, high ball in front of you is still a drive most of the time. One player off the line with a low, short ball is still a drop. Position tells you where the space is. Depth and height tell you whether you can actually hit it there.

### The Two-of-Three Rule

When all three reads agree, the decision is made for you. When they don’t, two out of three decides. Deep, high, and off the line is a drive. Short, low, and on the line is a drop. Anything mixed: count the reads, and go with the majority. The point isn’t which shot you prefer. It’s that you ran the checklist.

#### Four examples from a rec game

- Deep return, bounces high, returner still at midcourt. Three for drive. Hit it at the feet of the player who’s moving. This is the easiest point you’ll win all day and 3.5 players drop it out of habit.

- Short return, bounces low, both at the line. Three for drop. Step in, take it early, drop it into the kitchen, follow it in. Driving here is how you end up with a ball at your shoelaces.

- Deep return, bounces low, both at the line. One for drive (depth), two for drop (height, position). Drop it. This is the one that fools drivers, because it’s deep and “feels” like a drive. It isn’t.

- Short return, bounces high, returner off the line. One for drop (depth), two for drive (height, position). Drive it, at the player who’s moving. This is the one that fools droppers, because they’re close to the net and want to be gentle. Don’t be.

Self-check: in your next rec game, say the three reads out loud (or in your head) before every third shot: deep or short, high or low, on or off. If you can’t answer all three before contact, you’re still guessing. That’s the leak.

### Drive, Then Drop: The Fifth Shot

Quick count first: the serve is shot one, the return is shot two, your third shot is three, their reply is four, and the next ball your team hits is the fifth shot. So the “fifth shot” is just your second chance to get to the kitchen line.

A drive doesn’t have to win the point. Its job is to pull a weak ball out of your opponents so the fifth shot is an easy drop. Drive the third, read the block, drop the fifth, get to the line. This drive-and-drop sequence is how 4.0 players use the drive, and it’s why their drives look more effective than yours even when they aren’t hit harder.

#### How it works

When your drive is blocked back, it usually comes back softer and shorter than the original return. That’s a short, often low ball with your opponents now set at the line: two, sometimes three reads for drop. So you drop it. You didn’t change your mind. The reads changed, and you ran the checklist again.

#### The mistake

Driving the fifth because you drove the third. The block comes back, you’re fired up, you hit it again, and it goes into the net or gets counter-punched. Every ball gets its own three reads. The third shot doesn’t get a vote on the fifth.

### The Drill: 10 Minutes, Three Stages

Partner at the kitchen line feeding returns to you at the baseline. You call the read out loud before every ball, then hit the shot the checklist says. Ten balls per stage, count how many you called correctly and how many you executed. The goal is not perfect shots. The goal is a correct call on ten out of ten.

- Stage 1: one read at a time (10 balls). Your partner feeds deep or short on purpose and tells you which. You just call “deep” or “short” and hit the matching shot. Then do the same with high and low. You’re building the vocabulary.

- Stage 2: all three reads, partner sets the position (10 balls). Your partner feeds randomly and either stays at the line or backs up to midcourt before each feed. You call all three reads out loud, then hit. Count correct calls out of ten.

- Stage 3: live third-and-fifth (10 balls). Your partner feeds, you hit the third, they block it back, you hit the fifth, then follow it to the line. Two decisions per rally, both called out loud. This is the one that transfers to a real game.

Two sessions a week for a month. If your correct-call count isn’t at nine or ten out of ten by then, the problem is the reads, not the shots, and that’s something I can see on film in about two rallies.

Self-check: film ten of your third shots in a real game. For each one, pause before contact and score the three reads yourself. If your shot matched the checklist on fewer than seven of ten, run the drill before you work on anything else.

### What to Do Next

The third shot is one decision inside the first four shots, which is Leak 1 of five. If you’re not sure the third shot is your leak, the five-leaks article walks through all of them, and the free 17-question diagnosis scores you across all five and tells you which one is costing you the most points.

If you want my read on your specific third shot, that happens on Crestline: send footage, and I’ll tell you whether it’s the reads, the shot, or the feet, and what to drill first.

Get My Read on Your Game → Take the Free Diagnosis →

### Questions

Should I drive or drop my third shot in pickleball?

Read three things: depth of the return, height of the bounce, and whether your opponents are on the kitchen line or off it. Deep, high, and opponents off the line leans drive. Short, low, and opponents at the line leans drop. When the reads disagree, two out of three decides.

Why do my third shot drives keep getting blocked back at my feet?

Usually because you drove a ball you contacted below net height, or you drove into two players who were already set at the line. A lifted drive is the easiest ball in pickleball to block. Check the height and position reads before you swing; if either one says drop, drop.

Why do my third shot drops keep popping up?

Most often because you tried to drop a deep, high ball from behind the baseline, which is a long, hard drop, or because your feet were still moving at contact. A deep, high ball with a player off the line is a drive. Save the drop for short and low balls, and get your feet set before you hit it.

What is the drive-and-drop sequence in pickleball?

Drive the third shot to force a weak block, then drop the fifth shot into the kitchen and follow it to the line. The drive is not trying to win the point; it is setting up an easier drop. Each shot still gets its own three reads.

How do I practice the third shot decision, not just the shot?

Have a partner feed returns from the kitchen line while you call the three reads out loud before every ball, then hit what the checklist says. Score correct calls out of ten, not clean shots. Progress from single reads, to all three with your partner changing position, to live third-and-fifth rallies.

- Odom L. Why You’re Stuck at 3.5: Leak 3, the transition zone (what to do after the third shot). pickleballchiro.co, 2026.

# Pickleball Knee Pain: The 3-Stage Fix (article)

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/pickleball-knee-pain/

Dr. Lane Odom · The Pickleball Chiro

## Pickleball Knee Pain: The 3-Stage Fix

Foam rolling and rest keep the pain quiet for a week. Here’s why it comes back, and the system I use to actually fix it.

4.7 DUPR Doctor of Chiropractic PCI Certified Coach

By Dr. Lane Odom, DC · PCI Certified Coach · Published September 14, 2026 · 10 min read Reviewed by Dr. Lane Odom, DC · Last reviewed October 12, 2026

Educational content only. Not intended to diagnose or treat. Results vary. Consult your physician before beginning any exercise program.

Knee pain is one of the most common complaints I see in recreational players over 45, and on most courts I’m on, somebody is managing a nagging knee. The pain shows up at the knee, but in my experience the cause is usually not the knee itself. It’s upstream: weak hips, movement mechanics that overload the joint, and volume spikes. Fix the upstream problem and the knee tends to calm down and stay that way.

Most players try the same three things: foam roll the IT band, stretch and ice, take a week off. All three can make the knee feel better for a little while. None of them fix why it started hurting in the first place, so it comes right back the next time you play a full session. This guide is the 3-stage system I use with players to actually get it to stop, built for people who refuse to just stop playing.

I’m a Doctor of Chiropractic and I play at a 5.0 level myself, so I see this from both sides of the net. As a chiropractor, the knee is one of the most common complaints that walks through the door. As a player, I’ve watched the same pattern happen to partners and opponents for years: they manage the pain instead of fixing it, and it costs them a season instead of a few weeks. This is the framework I built to stop that cycle.

### Why the Pain Keeps Coming Back

Most players are treating the symptom, not the cause. Foam rolling, icing, and resting can all help temporarily. But if the actual cause never gets addressed, the knee flares up again the next time you go back to playing. The knee is where it hurts. The cause is almost always somewhere else in the chain.

The real problems are usually upstream: weak hips, poor movement mechanics, and volume spikes. Not the knee itself. Every low ball you dig out is a squat. Every lateral shuffle is a lunge. If your hips can’t do their job, the knee absorbs load it was never built to handle alone, and it lets you know.

This isn’t just a clinic observation. A 2015 systematic review in the British Journal of Sports Medicine found strong evidence that adding hip and glute rehab to knee-focused rehab reduced pain and improved function in people with patellofemoral (front-of-knee) pain, and that hip work alone beat quad work alone in the short and medium term.1 On the volume side, sports-science work on training load shows that injury risk climbs when the amount you do in a week jumps well above what your body has been used to, not simply when you play a lot.2 That’s the volume spike. And the number of senior pickleball injuries treated in U.S. emergency departments rose sharply from 2010 to 2019, approaching the count for senior tennis injuries by the end of that decade, with strains and sprains among the most common diagnoses, so this is not a small-scale problem.3

#### Why It Comes Back: Four Common Mistakes

- Treating only the symptom. Icing and resting without addressing the movement cause. It feels better, then it returns the moment you're back on court at full volume, because nothing about how you move actually changed.

- Returning too fast. Pain fades, so full play resumes immediately. The knee re-loads before it’s actually ready to handle it, and the same irritation shows back up within a week or two of hard play.

- Skipping hip strength. Weak glutes and hip stabilizers are the most common mechanical driver of recurring knee pain I see, and the stage most players skip because it doesn’t feel urgent once the pain is gone. It's the least exciting stage and the most important one.

- Stopping when it feels good. Strength requires maintenance. Pain relief is not the finish line, it’s the halfway point. The players who stay pain-free are the ones still doing the maintenance work months later.

Self-check: if your knee pain has come back more than once after resting it, you’re dealing with an upstream cause, not a knee problem. That’s exactly what the 3-stage system below is built to fix.

### Stage 1: Reduce Irritation

This doesn’t mean leave the court. It means reducing the load on the knee while keeping the body moving and waking up the muscles that should be doing more of the work. You don’t have to leave the court, just change how you use it while Stage 1 works.

Focus on four things: reduce match play volume without eliminating it, avoid explosive cuts temporarily, activate the hips and glutes starting day one, and drill instead of compete. None of that means sitting on the couch. It means being intentional about what you ask the knee to do while the tissue calms down and the hips start picking up more of the load.

Don’t start this program on your own if: the knee swelled up suddenly, it locks or gives way, the pain started with a fall or a collision, it wakes you up at night, or you can’t put weight on it. Those need to be evaluated in person first. This program is for the nagging, load-related knee that’s been building for weeks.

Not sure what an exercise looks like? Pictures and step-by-step instructions for every exercise on this page are in the free Knee Pain Guide.

#### Stage 1 Exercises — start here, 3–4x per week

- Modified Side Plank — activates the lateral hip, reduces the load the knee takes on every lateral cut and shuffle.

- Single Leg Glute Bridges — engages the glutes and teaches the hip to carry load so the knee doesn’t do all the work.

- Modified Copenhagen Plank — builds inner-thigh and hip control, stabilizes knee alignment during the split-step and shuffle.

- Fire Hydrants — targets the glute medius, the primary hip stabilizer that protects the knee during play.

You’re ready for Stage 2 when: walking and stairs are pain-free, all four Stage 1 exercises cause zero knee pain, and drilling feels comfortable.

### Stage 2: Build Strength

This is the stage most players skip. Pain fades, they return to full play, and it comes back within weeks because the knee never actually got the support it needed. The goal here is building the hip and glute strength that takes pressure off the knee during every lateral move, split-step, and push-off.

This is the difference between managing knee pain and actually fixing it. Stage 1 calms the tissue down. Stage 2 is where the knee gets stronger than it was before the pain started, which is the only thing that keeps it from coming back once you're playing full volume again.

#### Stage 2 Exercises — build the foundation, 3–4x per week

- Full Side / Copenhagen Plank — strengthens the hip abductors and adductors, controls leg alignment under every court stance and lunge.

- Single Leg Hip Thruster — builds the glute power that absorbs force before it reaches the knee on every push-off.

- Single Leg Step-Downs — trains the hip to stabilize the knee during the loading phase that happens before every shot.

- Kickstand RDLs — builds posterior chain and single-leg balance that transfers directly to court movement and deceleration.

You’re ready for Stage 3 when: Stage 2 exercises are pain-free and feel genuinely stronger, not just tolerable, and you can drill at real intensity without the knee reacting the next day.

### Stage 3: Return to Full Play

Pain is gone. Strength is built. Now we reintroduce the explosive demands of pickleball, gradually. Even once pain is gone, the knee still needs time to rebuild tolerance to the impact of competitive play, so this stage is a progression, not a light switch.

This is where I see the most players get impatient. Pain-free feels like the finish line, so they go from drilling straight back to three-hour tournament days. The knee has to rebuild tolerance to real match intensity the same way it rebuilt strength in Stage 2: gradually, with a plan, not all at once.

#### Return-to-Play Progression

Week

Volume

Focus

Week 1

2–3x/week, short sessions

Drilling only, no match play

Week 2

3x/week, 50% intensity

Add recreational open play

Week 3+

Gradually back to full volume

Full competitive play resumes

Typical progression, not a guarantee. Move faster or slower based on how the knee responds, and get it evaluated if it isn’t improving.

#### Stage 3 Exercises — build power, 2–3x per week

- Single Leg RDLs — single-leg stability and hip control that transfers directly to explosive court cuts and changes of direction.

- Heavy Farmer’s Carries — core and hip stability under load, trains the body to resist the lateral forces of competitive play.

- Bulgarian Split Squats — builds quad and glute strength in a lunge position that mirrors the split-step and court lunge.

- Single Leg Bounds — controlled plyometric loading that prepares the knee for the impact of full competitive play.

Self-check: if any part of this progression brings the knee pain back, that’s not a setback, it’s information. Drop back to the last pain-free week and rebuild from there instead of pushing through it.

### Maintenance: Keep These Forever

Strength requires maintenance. Pain relief is not the finish line. Keep these in rotation 1–2x per week for good, even once you feel completely normal: single-leg hip thrusters, side plank variations, Bulgarian split squats, single-leg RDLs.

#### The Quick Start Plan

Weeks

Stage

Focus

Week 1–2

Stage 1, 3–4x/wk

Reduce knee irritation, limit match play, drill and activate the hips

Week 3–4

Stage 2, 3–4x/wk

Build single-leg strength, reintroduce recreational play at reduced intensity

Week 5+

Stage 3, 2–3x/wk

Power and court readiness, return to full competitive play progressively

Typical progression, not a guarantee. Move faster or slower based on how the knee responds, and get it evaluated if it isn’t improving.

Consistency plus gradual progression is what keeps you on the court for the next 20 years, not the fastest possible return.

### What to Do Next

You have the framework. Pick the stage that matches where your knee is right now and start there, not at Stage 1 by default. If walking and stairs already don’t bother you, you may be ready to start in Stage 2. If you have no idea where to start, run the self-checks above in order until one of them tells you no.

If you want it in one place: the free guide covers Stages 1–3 with the full exercise breakdown you can save and follow along with.

One-time purchase, instant access, keep it forever. One PT session costs more than this. One missed tournament costs more than this.

### Questions

Is pickleball knee pain usually an IT band problem?

Usually not, even though the IT band is the first thing most players foam roll. The IT band can feel tight and sore because of what’s happening upstream: weak hips, movement mechanics that put extra load through the outside of the knee, or a recent jump in how much you’re playing. Foam rolling the IT band can feel good for a few hours, but if the hips and mechanics behind it never get addressed, the tightness comes right back.

Can I keep playing pickleball with knee pain?

In Stage 1, yes, in most cases. You don’t have to leave the court. You reduce match play volume, avoid explosive cuts temporarily, and drill instead of compete while you calm the knee down and activate the hips. The exception is pain that’s sharp, swelling, or getting worse each session. That’s a sign to get it looked at before you keep loading it.

How long does it take to fix pickleball knee pain?

It depends on the person. The Quick Start Plan is built as a five-week minimum: two weeks reducing irritation, two weeks building strength, then a gradual return to full play from week five on. How long it actually takes depends on how long the knee has been irritated, your starting strength, and how you respond to Stage 1, and some players need considerably longer. Consistency and gradual progression matter more than speed. Players who skip Stage 2 to rush back to full play are usually the ones back in my inbox a few weeks later. If the pain isn’t improving after a real attempt at Stages 1 and 2, get it evaluated in person.

Do I need an MRI for pickleball knee pain, or when should I see someone?

Most pickleball knee pain doesn’t need imaging to start working on it. This guide is educational content, not medical advice, so if pain is sharp, if the knee swells, locks, gives way, or if it isn’t responding after a real attempt at Stage 1 and Stage 2, that’s the point to see a licensed provider and get it properly evaluated instead of guessing further on your own.

Is my pickleball knee pain caused by my shoes?

Footwear can be a small piece of the puzzle, but it’s rarely the actual cause. The pattern I see over and over is weak hips, movement mechanics that load the knee wrong, and volume spikes, not the shoe on your foot. Before you spend money on new shoes, work the 3-stage system here. If the mechanics and strength are solid and something still feels off, footwear is worth a look.

- Gabbett TJ. The training-injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? Br J Sports Med. 2016;50(5):273-280. PubMed

- Weiss H, Dougherty J, DiMaggio C. Non-fatal senior pickleball and tennis-related injuries treated in United States emergency departments, 2010–2019. Inj Epidemiol. 2021;8:34. doi:10.1186/s40621-021-00327-9

A Bit About Me

### Tennis First, Then Pickleball

I grew up on a tennis court. I played competitive tennis for years, and racket sports have been part of my life for more than 13 of them. I picked up pickleball in 2023, right in the middle of chiropractic school at Palmer in Port Orange, and it took over fast. I still play tournaments around Florida, and I’ve brought home 20+ medals at 4.5 and up since I started.

What I like most about coaching is the moment a player sees on film what everyone has been trying to tell them. That’s why every team lesson I teach starts with your real games, and why so many of the players I coach come with the friends they play with every week.

Why I Do This

### Two Problems, One Coach

I was becoming an advanced pickleball player at the same time I was becoming a chiropractor. Training in both left me seeing the same problem from two directions. I'd watch players' bodies break down on the court, and in the same session I'd see exactly why they were stuck at the amateur level. Sometimes it was one or the other. A lot of the time it was both, and neither side was getting fixed because nobody was looking at the whole picture.

That's the gap I coach into. When I work with you, I'm looking at the whole chain your body uses to move and hit, from your legs up through your hips, core, and arm, to find the actual link that's costing you power or consistency. Sometimes that's a technique fix. Sometimes it's a real physical limitation we work around together. Either way it's one person looking at the whole picture, not a regular lesson or a regular clinic visit.

How I Coach

### Find the Leak First

Most players at 3.5 drill harder at the wrong thing. They take a lesson on the third shot drop when the real problem is that they're hitting a drop when the ball called for a drive, or they're already off balance before the ball gets there. So I don't start with a shot. I start by watching you play and finding the one pattern that costs you the most points. I call it your leak, and almost everyone has one big one, not ten small ones.

Then I teach the actual mechanic, fully. Not a tease, not a tip. If your third shot is the leak, you'll learn the read I use on every ball: how deep it is, how high it is, and whether it's on the line or off it, and what that combination tells you to hit. If your leak is the transition zone, you'll learn to read the other side's bodies instead of guessing when to move up. The mechanic is the same for everyone. What's specific to you is which one is holding you back, and that read is what I'm actually giving you.

Because I'm also a chiropractor, I notice the physical side of the leak while I'm coaching the technical side. A knee that won't load, hips that don't rotate, a shoulder that compensates. When that's in the way, we work on it directly instead of coaching around it forever.

Who I Work With

### 3.0 to 4.0 Players Who Are Stuck

The player I work with most is a 3.0 to 4.0 who plays on a league team or with a regular group. A few years in, holds their own at their level, has taken a lesson or two, and can't figure out why playing up feels a step too fast, or why the same team keeps beating them. A lot of my players come with their whole team, which is why the team lesson is the main thing I do. In plain words: 3.5 is the intermediate rating, 4.0 and up is where people start calling you advanced, and I coach the intermediate player who is trying to get there. That plateau is a specific problem with a specific set of causes, and I've built my coaching around it. If that's you, start with the free game diagnosis or read why players get stuck at 3.5.

On the chiropractic side, I see players and non-players across Volusia County who want hands-on care that includes rehab and corrective exercise, not just an adjustment. Pickleball knee pain, shoulders, and low backs make up most of it. If you're hurt, mobile chiropractic is the place to start.

# In-Person Pickleball Lessons

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/lessons/

#### How a Team Lesson Works

Right after the games: what I saw, while it’s still fresh.

- We play. Bring your team (4 to 8 players). We play real games while I film from the side.

- We fix it. For the rest of the hour I coach the weak spots I saw, on court, while it’s fresh.

- I break it down at home. I watch each pair’s film and talk through it on video, with timestamps. It goes up unedited, so you hear everything I see.

- You keep it. Your videos go into a private YouTube playlist and your notes into a Google Doc, so you can rewatch them before the next match.

### What You Actually Get

Most lessons teach a skill. I’d rather show you what’s happening in your real games, then fix that.

The Film

#### It Starts With Your Games

A drill can be the right skill for someone else’s game. I film how you actually play: where you stand, what you choose, and what happens when the score is close. Then we fix that.

Every Pair

#### Personal, Even in a Group of 8

To Keep

The Body

#### A Doctor Who Plays at a 5.0 Level

I’m a Doctor of Chiropractic, so I see the chain behind the shot: legs, hips, core, and arm. And I still compete at a 5.0 level, so what I coach is what I use.

The time behind one team lesson. An hour on court with you, then about an hour per pair once I’m home, putting together a video that usually runs 20 to 40 minutes. You’re getting about two hours of me, with notes and videos you keep.

I’m not aware of another coach in the area who films your team’s games and sends every pair its own breakdown.

Before You Book

### Questions

Which option should I pick?

If you play on a league team or with a regular group of 4 or more, pick the team lesson. It's the main thing I do. Not on a team? Get three to seven people you already play with and that's a team for this. If it's just you, or you and one or two friends, open the private and small-group section under Pricing. If you're not local, or want match film reviewed between lessons, try virtual coaching. Still not sure? Text me.

Isn't $70 a lot for a one-hour group lesson?

For a private lesson, $70 wouldn't raise an eyebrow. For a group of 4 to 8, I get why it might. Most big group lessons work on one skill for everyone, which might be your bottleneck or somebody else's. Here I film your own games and every pair gets its own breakdown, so the feedback is about you, even in a group of 8. It's the most personal group lesson you'll ever take. And it's more than an hour: after we're done on court, I spend about an hour on each pair's video. You're getting about two hours of me, with notes and videos you keep.

How is this different from a clinic or a club lesson?

A clinic or club lesson usually runs everyone through the same drills, and you hope it shows up in your next match. I start from your actual games: I film you playing, coach what I saw, and every pair leaves with a breakdown of its own film. More on that in how I coach differently from the average pickleball coach in Daytona Beach.

What do I get after the lesson?

Your team gets a private YouTube playlist with each pair's video and a Google Doc with your notes. In each video I watch your game and talk through it as it plays, pausing on the points that matter: where you're standing, which shot you chose, and what to do instead. They usually run 20 to 40 minutes, with timestamps so you can jump to your points. Everything opens on your phone with one tap, nothing to sign up for. There's a full example above.

I don't love being filmed. Who sees the videos?

Most people feel that way at first. I film from the side while you play your normal game, and after a few points nobody notices the camera. The film is how I give each of you personal feedback, so everyone plays on camera. It all stays private: only your team gets the playlist, and I never post anyone on social media unless they tell me I can.

My team has mixed levels. Is that OK?

Yes. Most league teams do. The film is per pair and I coach what I actually saw, so the strongest player and the newest player each leave with their own fix.

Who books and pays, and what if our roster changes?

One person, usually your captain, books the session. They can pay for everyone, or each player can pay me directly by Zelle, Venmo, or cash. Subs are welcome (whoever plays gets filmed), and one person missing doesn't sink it. If you'll have fewer than 4, tell me as early as you can and we'll sort it out. I ask for at least 12 hours' notice to cancel or reschedule.

Can you coach our team for the whole league season?

Yes. Message me with your league and schedule. We can do team lessons as often as you like, you can send me match footage for a game film review, or I can come film a match.

What do I get in a private or small-group lesson?

We pick one skill, go over the technique and drill it. You also get a short slow-motion video of a few reps of one shot, usually 2 to 3 minutes, with my biomechanical breakdown, and your 2 to 3 focuses for the week go in your portal. Private is $90 an hour; a small group of 2 to 3 players is $60 each.

Can I take lessons if I'm dealing with pain or an injury?

Usually, yes. That's where my chiropractic background helps most. I'll work around what hurts, and a lot of the time a mechanical issue in your stroke is feeding the pain. If something needs real treatment first, I'll tell you.

What level of player do you work with?

Mostly 3.0 to 4.0: intermediate (3.5) players who want to reach advanced (4.0+) play, many of them on league teams. Not sure where you fall? Just ask.

Where do you teach, and what should I bring?

Most lessons happen at Chipshot in Daytona Beach: indoor, air conditioned, and a court is always open. I also teach at public courts in New Smyrna Beach (Pettis Park is the most popular), Port Orange, Daytona Beach, and Ormond Beach. Some are packed in the mornings and some aren't, so tell me where and when your team plays and I'll match you with a court that's open. Just bring your paddle; I bring the balls, cameras, and a ball machine when we need it.

Ready?

# Pickleball Coach in Daytona Beach: How I'm Different From the Average Lesson

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/pickleball-coaches-daytona-beach/

Dr. Lane Odom · The Pickleball Chiro

## Pickleball Coach in Daytona Beach: How I’m Different

Plenty of good lessons around here teach the shots. This is what changes when you’re a 3.0–3.5 on a league team who wants to reach 4.0.

4.7 DUPR Doctor of Chiropractic PCI Certified Coach

By Dr. Lane Odom, DC · PCI Certified Coach · Published September 15, 2026 · 6 min read

Most pickleball lessons in the Daytona Beach area teach shots: grip, dinks, drops, a lot of fed balls. That’s the right tool while you’re still building strokes. It’s a different job once you have the strokes and keep losing the same points anyway. That second player is who I coach: intermediate (3.5) players who want to reach advanced (4.0+) play, most of them on league teams. I film your real games, find the one pattern costing you points, and fix the body mechanics behind it, not just the paddle. I play at a 5.0 level, I’m PCI certified, and I’m a licensed Doctor of Chiropractic.

### What a Typical Lesson Here Looks Like

Pickleball in Volusia County has grown fast, and most of the coaching has grown to match the biggest group of players: people who picked up a paddle in the last year or two. A typical lesson or clinic is an hour of fundamentals. Grip, ready position, serve and return, how to dink, a lot of balls fed from a bucket, some games at the end. It’s friendly and structured, and plenty of good coaches here run it well.

That’s not a knock. I bring lessons back down to that level myself when a backhand or footwork needs rebuilding from the ground up. Fundamentals are fundamentals.

What that format usually can’t do is look at your games. Everyone runs the same drill, whether it’s your problem or the problem of the player next to you. Nobody films you in a real game, counts where your lost points ended, or looks at why your reset pops up in the fourth game but not the first. For a newer player that’s fine, because the shots are the problem. For a 3.5 who has been stuck for six months, the shots are rarely the problem.

### What’s Different When You Train With Me

#### 1. We start with your real games, not a curriculum

The main thing I do is a team lesson for league teams and regular groups of 4 to 8. You play real games while I film from the side, then I spend the rest of the hour coaching the weak spots I saw. A 3.5 player almost always has one or two leaks, not ten, and most guess wrong about which ones. The player who thinks it’s their dinks usually has a transition-zone problem. The camera settles it in about two rallies. I wrote the whole framework up in Why You’re Stuck at 3.5: The Five Leaks, and there’s a free 17-question diagnosis if you want a first read before we ever meet.

#### 2. Every pair gets its own breakdown

After the lesson I go home and break down each pair’s film on video, usually 20 to 40 minutes with timestamps, pausing on the points that matter: where you were standing, which shot you chose, and what to hit instead. Your team gets the videos in a private YouTube playlist and your notes in a Google Doc, so you can rewatch them before your next match. Even in a group of 8, you hear about your own game. If it’s just you or a couple of friends, a private or small-group lesson works on one skill, and you get a short slow-motion clip of that shot with my breakdown.

A minute from a women’s 3.5 game I broke down: where to stand while your partner serves. Your team’s breakdowns look like this, on your own games.

#### 3. We look at the body behind the shot

This is the part no standard lesson can offer. I’m a licensed Doctor of Chiropractic (Palmer College of Chiropractic Florida, 2025) as well as a PCI Level 1 certified coach, so when a shot breaks down I can see whether it’s the technique, the feet, the hips, or the fact that your legs are gone by game four. A lot of “bad hands” at the kitchen is actually a trunk that isn’t set. A lot of popped-up resets are a knee that won’t bend under fatigue. When that’s the case, the fix is a movement pattern or a strength piece, and I can give you that too. If something hurts, there’s mobile chiropractic care that comes to you, and a full guide to pickleball knee pain.

#### 4. What I teach is what I’m using right now

I still compete: 4.7 DUPR, playing at a 5.0 level, with 20+ tournament medals at 4.5+ since 2023 and 13+ years of racket sports before that. The patterns I ask you to read are the ones I’m reading on Sunday. That matters for a 3.5 to 4.0 jump specifically, because the difference between those levels is decision-making under pressure, and it’s hard to coach a decision you don’t make yourself.

#### 5. The coaching continues between sessions

In-person lessons are one piece. Between them, you can send footage through Crestline and get a voice-and-video breakdown and a drill plan, from anywhere. Most of my players do a lesson, drill for two or three weeks, send a clip, and come back when the leak has moved. That’s faster and cheaper than a standing weekly lesson where you re-learn the same thing.

The short version: a standard lesson teaches you shots. I film your games, find the one pattern costing you points, fix the body mechanics behind it, and every pair leaves with its own breakdown. If you already have the shots and you’re still stuck, that’s the difference you’re paying for.

### Who I’m Not the Right Coach For

- Brand-new players. If you’ve played fewer than a dozen times, take a beginner class or a group clinic first. You need reps and friends more than you need a diagnosis, and you’ll get more per dollar from a group.

- Players who want a weekly hitting session. I’m happy to feed balls, and I have a ball machine, but if the goal is exercise and a good time rather than a rating jump, a standing social lesson elsewhere will suit you better.

- Players who want a quick tip and nothing else. The lesson finds the leak; practicing the fix is what moves your rating. It doesn’t take much, even ten minutes before rec play, but it does take some.

If that’s you, no hard feelings. Take the free diagnosis anyway; it’s useful at any level.

### Where and How Much

Chipshot in Daytona Beach is where most lessons happen. It’s indoor, air conditioned, and there’s always a court, so no rainouts and no waiting. I also teach at public courts around Volusia County when they’re not busy: Pettis Park in New Smyrna Beach is the most popular, and there are courts in Daytona Beach and Port Orange we can use during quieter hours. Tell me where you are and we’ll pick the spot that works.

$70 per player for a team lesson (league teams and regular groups of 4 to 8 players, with your games filmed and a video breakdown of each pair’s film afterward). $90 per hour for a private lesson, and $60 per person for a small-group lesson of two or three players. Full details on the lessons page; virtual coaching plans are on the virtual coaching page.

Book a Lesson → Take the Free Diagnosis →

### Questions

Who is the best pickleball coach in Daytona Beach for an intermediate player trying to reach 4.0?

It depends on what is actually holding you back, and most 3.5 players guess wrong about that. Look for a coach who will watch you play before telling you what to work on, who can explain why a shot breaks down under pressure and not just how to hit it, and who has played at the level you are trying to reach. That’s how I coach: I film your real games, I play at a 5.0 level, I’m PCI certified, and I’m a Doctor of Chiropractic, so lessons cover the shot and the body mechanics behind it. Most of my players come with their league team, and every pair gets its own video breakdown afterward.

How much do pickleball lessons cost in Daytona Beach?

Lessons in the Daytona Beach area are usually priced by the hour. I charge $70 per player for a team lesson (league teams and regular groups of 4 to 8 players, with your games filmed and a video breakdown of each pair’s film afterward), $90 an hour for a private lesson, and $60 per person for a small-group lesson of two or three players. Group clinics and community classes cost less per person and are the better value for beginners.

Where do pickleball lessons happen in Daytona Beach?

Most of my lessons happen at Chipshot in Daytona Beach, which is indoor and air conditioned with a court always available, so there are no rainouts. I also teach at public courts around Volusia County when they are not busy: Pettis Park in New Smyrna Beach is the most popular, and there are courts in Daytona Beach and Port Orange that work during quieter hours.

Should a beginner take private lessons or a clinic?

A beginner or a player under about 3.0 gets more from a class or clinic: you need reps, rules, and a friendly group more than you need diagnosis. Private lessons start paying off once you are a consistent 3.0 to 3.5 and losing the same kinds of points, because the thing holding you back is usually one specific pattern a coach has to see in your game.

What is different about a lesson with a chiropractor who coaches pickleball?

A standard lesson looks at the shot. I also look at the chain behind it: how your feet, hips, and trunk are set at contact, why a reset pops up when you are tired, why a knee or shoulder starts hurting in the fourth game. Because I’m a licensed Doctor of Chiropractic as well as a PCI certified coach, the fix can include the movement pattern, not just the paddle, and the drill you leave with is built for your body and your leak.

How many lessons does it take to go from 3.5 to 4.0 in pickleball?

Most 3.5 players do not need a long series of lessons. They need one or two sessions to find the leak, a ten-minute drill they can run twice a week, and a check-in a few weeks later to confirm it stuck. A few sessions spread over six to eight weeks is a realistic starting point. The more you practice the fix between sessions, even ten minutes before rec play, the faster it sticks.

### Questions

What does a mobile chiropractic visit look like?

First visit starts with a focused intake covering your history and goals, then we get to work the same visit. Every session includes a chiropractic adjustment, soft tissue work, and corrective exercise. Cupping and IASTM get added in as needed. First visits typically run 60 to 90 minutes. Wear comfortable clothes you can move in.

Do you offer multi-visit packages or an ongoing care plan?

Yes, but not as a fixed subscription. After your first visit I'll give you an honest read on what's going on clinically and how long I think it'll realistically take to resolve, then we build a plan around that together. Some people need one visit, some need several over a few months. It's arranged around your situation, not a flat monthly plan.

Do you come to my home, and do you take insurance?

Yes, I come to you: inside your home, the driveway, the garage, or the backyard. I bring everything, including a portable table. This is cash-pay care with no insurance billing, though some HSA and FSA plans cover chiropractic care, which is worth checking with your provider.

Do I need a referral for mobile chiropractic care?

No referral needed. Chiropractors are primary care providers in Florida, so you can book directly. I currently serve Daytona Beach, Ormond Beach, New Smyrna Beach, Port Orange, and Edgewater. Not sure if you're in range? Just ask.

How often will I need mobile chiropractic visits?

It depends on what's going on. I'll give you an honest clinical recommendation after the first visit, and we work within your schedule from there. Nobody gets a generic frequency without me actually looking at your case first.

What conditions does mobile chiropractic care treat?

Mostly musculoskeletal: back pain, neck pain, shoulder and hip issues, disc problems, sciatica, sports injuries, and headaches. If you're a pickleball player, I'm also looking at the movement chain behind whatever's bothering you, not just the spot that hurts.

What's the cancellation policy for mobile visits?

I ask for at least 12 hours notice to cancel or reschedule. If I'm already in transit or arrive and you're not available, the session is forfeited or a cancellation fee applies. Life happens, but a heads-up protects both of our time.

A 4.5 men's doubles match reviewed the way a Crestline submission gets reviewed: patterns, decisions, and the physical side of the game.

#### 4.5 Rec Play Game Analysis

Rec play at 4.5, analyzed for the one or two patterns that separate the players who keep climbing from the ones who stall.

Before You Sign Up

### Questions

How does virtual pickleball coaching work?

It runs on the three-step loop above: you upload footage through Crestline, I break it down and send feedback in the format your plan includes, then you get a drill plan built around exactly what showed up in that footage. Pro covers 2 reviews a month and Premium covers 4, about one a week, so pick the plan that matches how often you want feedback.

I'm not great with technology. Is this hard?

If you can take a video on your phone, you can do this. You film a game, open Crestline, and upload the video. My review comes back in the same place. If you get stuck on the first upload, message me and I'll walk you through it.

I don't like watching myself on video. Do I have to?

Almost nobody does at first. You don't have to study it: I watch the whole thing and tell you the one or two things that matter most. Seeing it once is usually when it clicks, because you can finally see what everyone's been telling you.

Is a review worth paying for?

Start with the free gameplay diagnosis and decide after. You get your own match broken down by someone who plays at a 5.0 level and knows the body, plus a plan for what to fix first. You can rewatch it as often as you like, which you can't do with a lesson you only hear once.

Do I need to live near Florida to work with you?

No, that's the point of this page. In-person lessons and mobile chiropractic care only run in Volusia County, FL, but footage review doesn't care where you're standing when you film it. If you do live nearby, in-person team lessons are still worth a look.

I already take a team lesson with you. Does this help?

Yes. It's the same breakdown I do after a team lesson, on a match you film yourself. Send a league match between sessions and you'll know whether the fix from the lesson is showing up when it counts.

What's included in a Crestline coaching program?

The pricing table above breaks down exactly what each plan includes. The short version: both monthly plans get voice-and-video footage review with a custom drill plan and priority replies. Pro covers 2 video reviews a month; Premium covers 4 and adds strength, rehab, and nutrition support. Start with the free gameplay diagnosis, then pick the plan that fits how much feedback you want.

What if I don't have game footage yet?

That's fine. Any video from your phone works to start, even a casual drill or practice game. No special camera or setup needed. Once I see how you move and play, I'll tell you exactly what to film next to get the most out of your review.

Can I switch or cancel my plan later?

Yes. Crestline virtual coaching is a monthly subscription you manage directly in your Crestline account, so you can change plans or cancel anytime before your next billing date.

# Why You're Stuck at 3.5 — Free Self-Diagnosis (quiz)

URL: https://pickleballchiro.co/quiz/

← pickleballchiro.co

Free Self-Diagnosis

## Why Are You Stuck at 3.5?

Your rating is an average. This takes about 3 minutes and shows you exactly which part of your game is dragging it down.

17 questions · No email required

### What This Diagnosis Covers

Fifteen scored questions across the five areas where 3.0–4.0 players leak the most points, plus two quick ones about where you play and who you’d train with, so your result points you to the right kind of coaching. Your answers are scored by category; the lowest-scoring one is the specific leak capping your rating right now.

#### First Four Shots

The serve, the return, the third shot, and the fourth. These four shots decide who reaches the kitchen line first, and most points between 3.0 and 4.0 players are effectively over before anyone gets there.

- When you serve, what usually happens?

- On your return of serve, where does the ball usually end up?

- Your third shot, the one that’s supposed to get you to the kitchen — what happens most often?

#### Shot Selection

Choosing the right shot for the ball you actually got: drive, drop, reset, or dink. A 3.5 player usually hits the shot they like; a 4.0 player hits the shot the ball height and position call for.

- When a ball comes at you below your waist, what’s your instinct?

- After you reset or dink, what usually happens next?

- How often do you feel like you “didn’t mean to hit it that hard,” or get caught off guard by your own shot?

#### Transition Zone

The space between the baseline and the kitchen line, roughly 7 to 15 feet from the net. Getting through it safely after the third shot, without getting stuck or rushing, is the single most common gap in a 3.5 game.

- After your third shot, what do you usually do?

- When a ball comes fast at your feet while you’re moving forward, what happens?

- How often do you feel like you’re “a step behind” during a point?

#### Kitchen / Soft Game

Dinking, resets, and handling speed-ups at the non-volley line. Points at the 4.0 level are won here, so a player who can’t sustain a dink rally or defend a speed-up can’t hold a lead against better opponents.

- Honest check: in a typical rec game, how often do you actually get to the kitchen line before the point is decided?

- A speed-up comes at you at the kitchen line — what usually happens?

- When you’re in a dink rally, what’s actually happening?

#### Physical

Whether your body can hold up your technique for a full session. Fatigue, stiffness, and old injuries change footwork and contact point in game three even when the mechanics looked fine in warmup. This is the part a coach who is also a chiropractor sees first.

- How does your game change between game one and game three of the same session?

- Do you do anything physical off the court (mobility, strength, conditioning) to support your game?

- Do you have any nagging stiffness, pain, or “that’s just how my body feels now” spots that affect how you move on court?

Built by Dr. Lane Odom, DC — Doctor of Chiropractic, PCI certified pickleball coach, 4.7 DUPR. Read the full breakdown of all five leaks in Why You’re Stuck at 3.5: The Five Leaks. Take the quiz above, or go straight to virtual coaching or in-person lessons in Volusia County, FL.
